claims.value: Murat found the rear guard of a corps of cavalry and infantry in position on the heights behind Erfurt and had it charged; the enemy cavalry fled and the town gave refuge to the infantry and the cavalry. As the infantry did not come, he had the place summoned, threatening to burn it, through Colonel Préval. Murat then reported that, in accordance with the capitulation, the dragoons had taken possession of the gates of Erfurt and handed them at once to the infantry of Ney's corps.

claims.value: Höpfner: the Prince of Orange had arrived in Erfurt, and after him Field Marshal Möllendorf, who had the prince assemble the generals and staff officers on the Petersberg; towards noon Möllendorf gave the definite order for the baggage to leave at once for Langensalza and the cavalry and the infantry to follow at set hours. General Larisch at once left his position on the Galgenberg with the infantry and fell back in disorder to the town. Having received the King's order to march to Sömmerda, Larisch resolved to carry it out at once, but the prince had him halt and, on the Petersberg, repeated the order, since getting through was no longer possible; when Larisch appealed to the King's order, the prince gave the strict order that he stay in Erfurt with the troops and have the walls manned. The commandant, Major Prüschenk, at first meant to defend himself seriously but soon changed his mind; Möllendorf attended only the start of the negotiations. The prince dictated the points of the capitulation to Major Lossau of the general staff. Höpfner judges that not defending the town was in order, but that it would then have been a duty to take the troops out at once to continue the retreat under the Duke of Weimar's protection, and that the surrender of the Petersberg was irresponsible: against a regular attack it could have held out 19 days.
claims.rationale: Side B's decisions in side B's history, with its judgments, which are evaluations, not measured effects. Préval's letter has the prince and Möllendorf ask to march out with arms, baggage and battalion guns rather than become prisoners of war (claim side-b-objectives). claims.value: Bodart records the capitulation of Erfurt on 15 October: the Prussian troops marched out with the honours of war, laid down their arms on the glacis and became prisoners of war; the officers, among them a field marshal and six generals, were released on their word not to serve against France until exchanged. Höpfner says the capitulation was concluded in the night to the 16th; men from the Bayreuth country were sent home and the rest treated as prisoners of war. The terms the major general sent Murat as the only capitulation His Majesty could grant were that the troops march out with the honours of war, file through the middle of the French army and lay down their arms, the soldiers keeping their booty and the officers their baggage; all were to be prisoners of war, the soldiers and even the generals to be sent to France, though the Emperor left Murat latitude to let the officers go home on their undertaking not to serve before their exchange. Murat reported on the 16th that the capitulation had been entirely executed.
claims.rationale: The frozen frame outcome with the agreeing accounts; no source read gives a different result. The capitulation's own text was not found in the passages read. Bodart dates the entry the 15th and Höpfner the conclusion the night to the 16th. English renderings (ours): Bodart, 'the Prussian troops were allowed to march out with the honours of war, but had to lay down their arms on the glacis and give themselves up as prisoners of war'; 'the officers (among them 1 field marshal, 6 generals) were granted free departure against the obligation on their word of honour not to serve against France before their exchange'; Höpfner, 'and in the night to the 16th the capitulation was indeed concluded'; 'all the men from the Bayreuth country were sent home, the rest regarded as prisoners of war' (OCR); the major general, 'here is the only capitulation His Majesty can grant: the troops will march out with the honours of war, file through the middle of the French army, lay down their arms. The soldiers will keep their booty, the officers their baggage; they will all be prisoners of war; the soldiers will go to France; even the generals will have to be sent there; however the Emperor leaves you the latitude to' (OCR); 'allow the officers to go home with the undertaking not to serve before their exchange' (OCR); Murat, 'Erfurt, 16 October 1806'; 'I have the honour to report to Your Majesty that the capitulation is entirely executed'.

claims.value: Side B's aims: towards noon Möllendorf gave the definite order for the baggage to leave at once for Langensalza and the cavalry and the infantry to follow at set hours; soon after noon a courier brought the order for the retreating troops to go to Sömmerda, which reached General Larisch in the town as the King's order. The Prince of Orange instead had Larisch stay in Erfurt and man the walls. In the negotiations, by Préval's report, the prince and Möllendorf asked to march out with arms, baggage and battalion guns rather than be made prisoners of war by a capitulation that would stain their reputation.
claims.rationale: Side B's aims from Höpfner and Préval's report (OCR passages); the reasons for the prince's order to stay are given only as his statement that getting through was no longer possible. English renderings (ours): Höpfner, as in claim side-b-command for Möllendorf's order (OCR); 'soon after noon the Feldjäger Horster came to Erfurt with the order to the retreating troops to go to Sömmerda' (OCR); 'General Larisch, to whom the King's order to march to Sömmerda had come directly in the town' (OCR); as in claim side-b-command for the order to stay (OCR); Préval, as in claim erfurt-ground for the heading (OCR); 'the Prince of Orange and His Excellency Marshal Möllendorf expect from Your Highness's generosity not to require that they stain their reputation by a capitulation that would make them, and their garrison, prisoners of war; they ask to march out with arms, baggage and battalion guns' (OCR).

claims.value: Side A attacked: Murat had the Prussian rear guard on the heights behind Erfurt charged, the enemy cavalry fled and the town gave refuge to the infantry and the cavalry; the French, held off by some cannon shots, brought up horse artillery and fired on the Johannes gate; Captain Baillot, with a dragoon division in pursuit, fired on a Prussian column making for the town, and the howitzers of two dragoon divisions bombarded the town until night against the fire of the ramparts; the place was then summoned. Side B's cavalry advanced against the enemy to cover the infantry's retreat to the town, and its resistance could only be short.
claims.rationale: Both sides' accounts describe the French attacking and summoning and side B falling back into the town and capitulating; the French artillery fire is from General Rott's report on the artillery of the reserves, printed in a footnote. The phase is left unresolved: the passages read show Murat's pursuit and the summons, but no order from above to attack Erfurt itself; the major general's letters written after the summons expect the taking of Erfurt and set the terms (claim side-a-objectives). English renderings (ours): Murat, as in claim side-a-command for the charge, the flight and the summons (OCR); Höpfner, 'some cannon shots stopped the enemy's further pursuit; he brought up horse artillery and fired on the Johannes gate of Erfurt' (OCR); Rott, 'General Rott, commanding the artillery of the reserve corps, to General Songis' (OCR); 'on ... October, the ... dragoon division pursuing the enemy retreating on Erfurt, Captain Baillot received the order to fire on a Prussian column heading for the town; which was carried out with enough success to hasten that column's retreat and make it abandon part of its baggage' (OCR); 'some hours later, the howitzer of this division and that of the ... dragoon division, commanded by Captain Churlaud, placed themselves in battery within good range of the town, threw a fairly considerable quantity of shells into it and, although entirely uncovered, kept up their fire until night against that of the ramparts' (OCR); Höpfner, 'while the cavalry mounted and advanced against the enemy to cover the retreat of the infantry. The enemy soon pressed forward with such superior cavalry that, with such exhausted strength, the resistance could only be short' (OCR).

claims.value: Side B held a fortified town: the Petersberg citadel, armed with 65 guns, and the Cyriaksburg had been put in a state of defence, though the Cyriaksburg was of little strength, the town's drawbridges and gates were not in order and its ditches were partly dry and fordable. Murat called Erfurt a place safe from a coup de main with a good citadel, and Préval described the citadel as well armed and palisaded.
claims.rationale: Coded B_fortified: the works were permanent fortifications held by side B and put in a state of defence before the action, so the claim is tagged inherited. A coding that counted only the fight on the heights before the town, where no works are named, would give none_named. English renderings (ours): as in claims erfurt-ground and means-and-supply.

open_questions: Deferred: the text of the capitulation itself, which the passages read do not print; the records of the Prussian judicial inquiries held after the war, on which by the preface of his first volume Höpfner's work chiefly rests; French returns of the prisoners and of the artillery and stores taken; a plan of Erfurt and its citadels. Figures seen only in the OCR and not restated: the hour of Murat's letter from before Erfurt of the 15th and its figures for the garrison and the guns in battery (Foucart t. II, pp. 19-20), the number of officers whose return on parole Murat granted (p. 20), the major general's figure for the men in Erfurt and Murat's for the prisoners on the 16th (pp. 36, 39), the hours in Murat's letter from the bivouac of the 16th (pp. 21-22), Höpfner's hours for Möllendorf's order, Préval's arrival and Ney's infantry (pp. 17, 18, 20), and the hour in the dateline of Murat's letter of the 16th on p. 47, which the page image leaves uncertain (8 or 3).

Most consequential gap: side B's strength and its composition at the surrender. Höpfner's 10,000 (and Bodart's) is the number taken, his units are not totalled, and Murat's estimates range from 6,000 to 7,000 surrendered to at least 6,000 prisoners and 5,000 wounded; a Prussian or French return of the prisoners could close it. Side A's strength before the town is unknown.

Disputes kept as separate claims: the men taken as 10,000 (Höpfner, Bodart), 6,000 to 7,000 surrendered, or at least 6,000 prisoners and 5,000 wounded (Murat); the guns as 65 (Bodart; Höpfner's armament of the Petersberg) or 60 in battery and 20 to 25 battalion guns (Murat); Ney's infantry's arrival in the evening at different hours in Höpfner and Murat (OCR).

Families and dependence: Bodart (a compilation; his sources for this entry were not checked, though his 65 guns match Höpfner's armament of the Petersberg); Foucart, t. II (the French side's documents: Murat's, Préval's, the major general's and the Emperor's letters and General Rott's report, interested accounts); Höpfner, Bd. 2, 2nd edition (the Prussian side's history; by the preface of his first volume the work rests chiefly on the records of the judicial inquiries held after the war into those who fell into captivity by capitulation or otherwise, but the passages read on Erfurt do not name their sources).
